opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd describe it as a successful proof of concept, but not a finished product, and I try to be upfront about that.

We had essentially one shot. When you're running at that scale on a shared supercomputer with a small team, you don't get the luxury of a dozen ablation runs at full size and then picking the best one. We did a lot of small-scale experiments beforehand, and frankly some of our early attempts at scaling up failed. The model would collapse or stop actually using its recurrence. Then we committed to a configuration and let it train. So there's a fair amount of "this is what we got" rather than "this is the optimal version of the idea."

What I'm happy with is that the central claim holds up. The model really does learn to use its depth at test time. If you let it iterate more in its latent space, its performance on reasoning-heavy tasks like math and code goes up, sometimes quite substantially. It does that without generating extra tokens and without being trained on any chain-of-thought data. That was the thing we wanted to show: that you can scale compute at inference in latent space rather than only by writing longer outputs.

What I'm more cautious about is the absolute performance. Compared to frontier models trained on far more data with much more polished recipes, it's obviously not competitive. Our data mixture was a reasonable guess, the training wasn't especially long by modern standards, and there was no real post-training. So if someone asks, "Is this the best model at its size?", the answer is no. If they ask, "Does this architecture do something interesting that standard transformers don't?", I think the answer is clearly yes.

I also find it scientifically fun because the model shows behaviors we didn't explicitly design. You can see different kinds of dynamics in the latent trajectories depending on the token, for example some that converge quickly and some that orbit. That suggests it's learning its own ways of using the recurrent computation.

So my overall assessment is that it's a promising first data point. It's good enough to justify taking the approach seriously, and rough enough that there's clearly a lot of headroom if someone puts real resources and iteration behind it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think of it as a proof of concept more than a finished product. We trained a 3.5 billion parameter model, which by today's standards is small, and we got exactly one shot at it. There was no hyperparameter sweep, no second run to fix the things we learned the hard way. So when I look at the model, I see a lot of warts that I know are there because we didn't get to iterate.

That said, the thing we actually wanted to test worked. The question was whether you could train a model that scales its reasoning by looping a recurrent block in latent space, rather than by generating more tokens, and whether that would be stable at scale. And it was. The model gets better the more times you let it recur at test time, and it does so on problems where you'd expect reasoning to matter, like math and code, more than on pure knowledge recall. That's the behavior we were hoping to see, and seeing it emerge in a single run on a modest compute budget told us the idea is real.

So if you ask me how good it is as a language model, I'd say it's roughly in the range of other open models trained on a similar token count, which is fine but not spectacular. If you ask whether the architecture does what we claimed, I'd say the evidence is much stronger than I expected going in. And frankly, the fact that a small team could pull this off on a single run says something about how much low-hanging fruit there still is outside the standard transformer recipe.

We have one result, rather than a whole series of experiments where we can isolate each decision. So I’d distinguish between being pleased with the model we produced as a small team and claiming that we’ve found the best recipe. The latter would take a lot more experimentation.

sol-6.1.text: I’d say it’s a promising first result, but I’d be careful about drawing strong conclusions from a single training run. With a small team, getting the whole pipeline to work is already meaningful. The next question is whether the choices we made consistently improve the model, and that takes more experiments. So I’d view it as a starting point rather than a finished statement about what we can achieve.
